title: Letters close
hook: sixty letters read of one hundred and twenty-four

segments.voice: Yesterday: imago vitae, the flawed man who left his friends the image of his life. Your line was flawed and wise. Where did you tuck the line you chose? Day four hundred ninety-four.

The letters open the same way. In Latin: Seneca Lucilio suo salutem. Seneca greets his Lucilius. Not Lucilius. His Lucilius. And they close with a single word: vale. Be well. Farewell. About two months ago we opened the first one, with an old man in Italy writing to a friend in Sicily about how to hold an hour. Today we fold the stack. Of the one hundred and twenty-four letters that survive, we've read from sixty. Tomorrow Seneca's essays begin. But first, one last look at the pile on the table. Today: letters close.
screen: `SENECA GREETS HIS LUCILIUS.` → `VALE: BE WELL.` → `SIXTY OF ONE HUNDRED TWENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: First, what was in the stack. Hold every hour. Who is poor. Choose, then trust. All mine is with me, said Stilpo, who'd lost everything. They're people, not just slaves. Harpaste, where the blindness is ours. Ictus animi and its first jolt. Apes. Cleanthes. Ratio. Sixty letters, and each left a line short enough to carry. Second, the little gifts. In the early letters, Seneca keeps ending with a saying he's found, often from Epicurus, a rival school. He calls it his daily payment to Lucilius. A teacher who takes good lines from wherever they grow: that's this whole path's method too. Third, the missing half. We have none of Lucilius' replies. Not one. Seneca answers questions we never hear asked. Scholars even debate whether this was a real exchange or a book written in the shape of letters, or some of each. The sources are silent, and we're left reading one side of a phone call. Fourth, why that's a gift. Because the empty half is where the reader sits. For sixty days, you've been Lucilius: the friend being written to, scolded, encouraged, sent a line at the bottom of the page. Every letter ended with vale, and waited. Tonight you get to answer.
screen: `SIXTY LETTERS, SHORT LINES TO CARRY.` · `A DAILY PAYMENT, OFTEN FROM EPICURUS.` · `NONE OF LUCILIUS' REPLIES SURVIVE.` · `THE EMPTY HALF IS YOURS.` · then, large: `WRITE BACK.`

segments.voice: Start a letter in your head, or on paper if you have it. Dear Seneca. Then three short things. One line of his that helped. One thing you tried because of him. And one place you'd push back: on the wealth, the court, the harsh consolation, anything. Be honest; he was. If you like, end the way he always did: vale. Be well. Let the letter sit in you until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Vale. The word that closes every one of Seneca's letters: be well, farewell, after sixty read of the one hundred twenty-four that survive. Today's word.
Your line: write back. Put your letter to Seneca on paper today, even four lines, and sign it. Keep it with the line you saved yesterday. Day four hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Some readers finish Seneca's letters by writing a letter back to him, naming what helped, what they tried and where they disagree.

options: read all sixty again at once.

original.note: Latin, 'be well': the word that closes every one of Seneca's letters.

trapdoor: what you thought: these were private letters someone found.
what it means: they're one side of a friendship, and the reader sits in the empty half.

what a scholar hears: whether the letters were truly sent is debated; their shape, opening greeting, a daily saying, vale, follows real Roman letters, while their order and polish suggest a book meant for readers.
